title: Beware the Facebook Parents' Group
author: Arthur Brooks
source: The Free Press, The Pursuit of Happiness with Arthur (thefp.com), August 17, 2026
summary: Arthur Brooks opens with a vivid personal anecdote, using Facebook to track down and rescue his adult son, an active-duty Marine, after a chaotic night in Las Vegas involving a casino dispute and stolen pants, to set up a more serious question he was asked after a speech on social media's costs to families: should a parent sending a first child off to college join an online parents' group? The piece uses the contrast between his own successful, narrow, purpose-driven use of social media (locating a specific person in an emergency) and the more diffuse, ongoing use represented by a parents' group to interrogate whether these platforms actually make parents' or children's lives better. Brooks frames the question as genuinely open rather than settled, acknowledging his own use of the technology even as he has spoken publicly about its dangers for families, and sets up an examination of what online parents' groups actually deliver versus what they promise. The piece is characteristic of Brooks's recurring argument that the value of a technology for family life depends heavily on the specificity and purpose of its use, rather than on the platform itself.
points: Opens with a concrete emergency-use case for Facebook (locating an active-duty Marine son during a crisis in Las Vegas within five minutes) to establish that the platform can serve a legitimate, narrow, high-stakes parenting function.

Frames the central question as coming directly from an audience member facing a specific, common parenting threshold moment: whether to join an online parents' group as her first child leaves for college.

Distinguishes purpose-driven, time-limited social media use (emergency contact) from open-ended, ongoing platform membership (a parents' group), setting up a sharper test than a blanket 'social media is bad for families' framing.

Acknowledges his own social media use even while having spoken publicly about the harms of overuse for families, positioning the piece as an honest reckoning with a nuanced answer rather than a simple prohibition.

Uses a real family story rather than an abstract argument to open the discussion, grounding the parents'-group question in the same household where the author has direct personal stakes and experience.
quotes: One Sunday night in 2022, our middle son, then still on active duty in the U.S. Marine Corps, called on a borrowed phone from Las Vegas, in need of assistance. His predicament included losses at the blackjack table, a difference of opinion with casino security about whether he should remain in the establishment, and, somehow, the theft of his pants.

Using the app, we were able to track down the profile of one of his Marine friends partying in Vegas, and in fewer than five minutes, we were direct-messaging him our son's whereabouts. Once reunited, the band of brothers hunted down the pants-stealing miscreant and administered justice.
What's a parent to do? Go on Facebook, of course. I recounted that story recently after a speech I gave about the problems that overuse of social media can cause for families.

I recounted that story recently after a speech I gave about the problems that overuse of social media can cause for families. An audience member had asked me whether I saw any ways that parents could use these applications to make their children's lives better, and whether I had done so myself.
She was sending her first child off to college and simply wondering how I felt about online parents' groups, which are generally hosted on Facebook. She wanted to know: Should she join one?
